# The Fixed Point

The trouble with keeping a lighthouse, Maren Sollis had told her daughter once, years before the silence fell between them, was that you never saw what you'd done. The ships that passed safely in the night didn't come back to thank you. The rocks that failed to claim them didn't testify. You kept the light, and the light kept them, and none of it was ever confirmed. You simply had to believe.

Sarah had been twelve then, sitting on the iron stairs with her knees pulled to her chest, watching her mother polish the Fresnel lens with the careful circular motion she'd been taught in her first week on the job. It was a summer visit — the only kind Sarah made after the divorce sent Maren to Tern Rock and sent Sarah to her father's house in Portland, where there were proper schools and proper seasons and girls her age who didn't think it was normal to live on a rock in the Atlantic.

"Don't you get lonely?" Sarah had asked.

"I get everything," Maren had said, which was not an answer.

---

Twenty-eight years. That was how long she'd been at Tern Rock, out past the mouth of Cadigan Bay, where the shipping lanes bent north toward the Canadian maritime and the weather came in cold and sideways from November through April. She had been thirty-four when she arrived, which meant she was sixty-two now, which she found it difficult to believe. The years on the rock had a way of collapsing into each other. Summer was a brightness. Winter was the work.

She'd been assigned the station by the Maritime Authority after her predecessor, a man named Dutch Haverford, had quietly retired to a cottage in Vermont and never looked at the ocean again. She'd applied on a whim, or what she called a whim, though her therapist at the time had called it something else. A retreat. A calculated disappearance. Her marriage had ended. She'd quit her job as a cartographer's assistant in Boston. She had thirty-four dollars, a duffle bag, and a need she could not have named precisely — to be somewhere that had clear rules. The light must burn. The lens must turn. The log must be kept.

She had not expected to stay more than two years.

She had not expected a great many things.

---

The storm on the twenty-third of November announced itself at three in the afternoon as a particular shade of greenish-gray low on the horizon, the kind of color that meant business. Maren had seen it a thousand times. She went through her preparations methodically: secured the mooring lines on the supply tender, closed and latched the storm shutters on the keeper's cottage, checked the fuel reserves, ran a test sequence on the light. The Maritime Authority had installed an automated system six years ago, a retrofit that was supposed to make her position redundant but somehow hadn't. She suspected it was because nobody else wanted to live out here in order to maintain it when it failed, which it did with some regularity and never at convenient moments.

Tonight, running through the test sequence, she noticed a flicker. Not in the light itself — the lamp rotated and pulsed correctly, its four-second rhythm unchanged — but in the timing mechanism, a digital stutter she'd seen once before the previous January. The display read 3.97 seconds between pulses instead of 4.00. A tenth of a second's variance. A tenth of a second, she knew from her training, could mean the difference between a navigator recognizing a light and not.
